mentions.quote: *Strīdhana* belongs to her offspring, and a daughter is a sharer in it
mentions.role: subject of inheritance rule

entities.description: The legally recognized category of property belonging exclusively to a woman, heritable by her offspring.
entities.justification: Directly named and defined as a category of property in Brh_1,26.31, with specific rules about who inherits it.

mentions.quote: It is ordained for those learned Brahmins who offer the funeral cake to him
mentions.role: ritual officiants entitled to ancestral property

mentions.quote: Sons of a Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, and Shudra wife, born of a Brahmin
mentions.role: caste category in inheritance apportionment

mentions.quote: A twice-born son shall obtain all; thus the *dharma* is established
mentions.role: privileged inheritor

mentions.quote: For a Brahmin, branding on the forehead is ordained; no other punishment
mentions.role: recipient of exceptional legal treatment

entities.description: The priestly Brahmin caste, who receive the largest inheritance shares among sons of mixed-caste unions and are exempt from corporal punishment.
entities.justification: Repeatedly invoked as the normative standard for property shares and as the exceptional case in penal law across multiple verses in this window.

mentions.quote: Sons of a Kshatriya wife take three, two, and one share
mentions.role: caste tier in inheritance formula

mentions.quote: For those Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras who are sonless and devoid of wife and brother, the king is the taker of their wealth
mentions.role: caste subject to royal escheat

mentions.quote: A son born of a Kshatriya wife by a Brahmin, who is eldest by birth
mentions.role: subject of inter-caste inheritance rule

entities.description: The warrior-ruler caste, whose sons receive a ranked intermediate share in Brahmin father's estate and whose property escheats to the king if they die without heirs.
entities.justification: Cited in several verses as a distinct legal tier within inheritance law alongside Brahmin and Vaishya.

mentions.quote: sons of a Vaishya wife take two and one share
mentions.role: caste tier in inheritance formula

mentions.quote: For those Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras who are sonless
mentions.role: caste subject to royal escheat

entities.description: The merchant-farmer caste, whose sons by a Brahmin father receive shares lower than Kshatriya sons but above Shudra sons.
entities.justification: Named alongside Kshatriya and Shudra in two distinct legal contexts — share allocation and royal escheat — establishing it as a defined legal category.

mentions.quote: A son born of a Shudra woman by one of the twice-born does not deserve a share of the land
mentions.role: excluded caste in land inheritance

mentions.quote: The son by a Shudra woman, the self-given son
mentions.role: subordinate heir category

mentions.quote: to the brother who is the son of a Shudra concubine, they should give a mere token of respect
mentions.role: son with minimal inheritance right

mentions.quote: For those Kshatriyas, Vaishyas, and Shudras who are sonless
mentions.role: caste subject to royal escheat

entities.description: The servile fourth caste, whose sons by twice-born fathers are systematically excluded from land inheritance and restricted to token maintenance.
entities.justification: The Shudra is the most legally disadvantaged caste category in the inheritance sections of this window, repeatedly named in rules that curtail or eliminate property rights.

mentions.quote: A Niṣāda who is the only son of a Brahmin is a sharer of a third part
mentions.role: mixed-caste heir with partial inheritance right

entities.description: A mixed-caste group (offspring of a Brahmin father and Shudra mother), granted only one-third of the estate even as sole son.
entities.justification: Named explicitly in Brh_1,26.123 as a distinct legal category with a defined fractional inheritance entitlement.

mentions.quote: Having worshipped Agni and Prajāpati, she is made so, said Gautama
mentions.role: deity invoked in the rite of appointing a daughter as son-substitute

entities.description: The Vedic fire deity, invoked alongside Prajāpati in the ritual that creates an appointed daughter (*putrikā*) as a substitute heir.
entities.justification: Named as one of two deities whose worship constitutes the consecration rite by which a daughter is appointed as heir, per Gautama's testimony.

mentions.quote: Having worshipped Agni and Prajāpati, she is made so, said Gautama
mentions.role: deity invoked in the rite of appointing a daughter as son-substitute

entities.description: The Vedic lord of creatures, invoked alongside Agni in the ritual consecration of an appointed daughter as heir.
entities.justification: Co-named with Agni in Brh_1,26.76 as the divine witness of the appointed-daughter rite, grounding its ritual legitimacy.

mentions.quote: Because a son saves his father from the hell called Put
mentions.role: afterlife punishment from which a son rescues his father

entities.description: The Dharmaśāstra hell reserved for men who die without a son, from which a son's birth and rituals are said to liberate the father.
entities.justification: Explicitly named in Brh_1,26.81 as the eschatological rationale for begetting sons — the etymological basis for the Sanskrit word *putra* (son).

mentions.quote: Someone who will go to Gayā, he will save us
mentions.role: sacred pilgrimage site associated with ancestral liberation

entities.description: A sacred pilgrimage site in the Gangetic plain where śrāddha offerings are held to be supremely efficacious for liberating ancestors.
entities.justification: Named in Brh_1,26.89 as the specific destination that ancestors hope a son will visit to offer liberating rites on their behalf.

mentions.quote: rites such as the Vaiśvadeva must be done by the undivided
mentions.role: household rite binding undivided family members

entities.description: The daily Vaiśvadeva fire rite performed in honor of all gods, cited here as a ritual obligation that presupposes an undivided household.
entities.justification: Named in Brh_1,26.145 as the paradigmatic undivided-family rite whose performance marks a household as legally undivided.

mentions.quote: all of them are called friends, *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha*, there is no doubt
mentions.role: legal classification for certain secondary sons

mentions.quote: by that misconduct he is a *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha*, there is no doubt
mentions.role: status assigned to one who abandons his family

entities.description: A legal-moral category denoting a person of doubtful or compromised family affiliation — applied both to certain son-types and to men who leave their natal family.
entities.justification: Defined and applied across two verses (Brh_1,26.74–75), making it a technical term in Bṛhaspati's classification of sons and social deviants.

mentions.quote: It is ordained for those learned Brahmins who offer the funeral cake to him
mentions.role: rite that legitimizes inheritance

mentions.quote: he will give the śrāddha daily
mentions.role: son's ritual duty cited as justification for begetting sons

mentions.quote: she should cause the monthly, six-monthly, and other śrāddhas to be offered
mentions.role: obligation of a widow who inherits

mentions.quote: having performed the funeral cake rite together, should then perform the rite for prosperity
mentions.role: prerequisite ritual act before partition

entities.description: The Brahminical ancestral offering rite — involving food, water, and fire — that is the ritual obligation binding heirs to the deceased and structuring the entire inheritance system.
entities.justification: Recurs throughout the window as the primary ritual justification for inheritance entitlement, widow's maintenance, and the necessity of having sons.

mentions.quote: Gambling was forbidden by Manu as it destroys truth, purity, and wealth
mentions.role: authoritative prior lawgiver whose ruling is cited

mentions.quote: Thirteen sons have been stated by Manu of old
mentions.role: source authority for the classification of sons

mentions.quote: the pre-eminence of Manu is remembered. A Smṛti that is contrary to the meaning of Manu is not to be praised
mentions.role: supreme standard against which all other Smṛti is measured

entities.description: The primordial lawgiver (*Manusmṛti*) invoked as the supreme authority in dharmaśāstra, whose rulings on sons, gambling, and the Veda establish the benchmark for all Smṛti texts.
entities.justification: Cited by name three times in distinct legal contexts — classification of sons, gambling prohibition, and the closing doxological statement — establishing him as the pre-eminent normative reference point.

mentions.quote: Having worshipped Agni and Prajāpati, she is made so, said Gautama
mentions.role: cited authority on the appointed-daughter rite

entities.description: The Dharmasūtra author Gautama, cited as the source for the ritual procedure of creating an appointed daughter.
entities.justification: Named in Brh_1,26.76 as the authority for a specific ritual ruling on the *putrikā* rite, functioning as a citation to the *Gautamadharmasūtra*.

mentions.quote: all of it for one without son, father, or wife—thus says Śaunaka
mentions.role: cited authority on the cremator's share

entities.description: The Vedic-ritual authority Śaunaka, cited as the source for the rule governing how much of a deceased person's estate a non-kin cremator may take.
entities.justification: Named by the attribution formula 'thus says Śaunaka' in Brh_1,29.11, marking him as an external authority whose ruling is being incorporated into Bṛhaspati's text.

themes.topic: Inheritance and partition of family property

mentions.quote: without assembling all the sons, there should be no gift and no sale
Those two who have reunited out of affection are sharers of each other's property
A document of proclamation should be made by partitioned brothers among themselves

themes.justification: The dominant legal subject of this window, spanning rules on who may divide property, in what shares, under what conditions — constituting the bulk of chapter 1.26.

themes.topic: Caste hierarchy as the determinant of inheritance shares

mentions.quote: Sons of a Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, and Shudra wife, born of a Brahmin, in order, should take four, three, two, and one share respectively
A son born of a Shudra woman by one of the twice-born does not deserve a share of the land

themes.justification: A recurrent structural logic throughout the window: the mother's caste rank directly determines the fraction of the father's estate her son receives, making caste the key variable in property law.

themes.topic: Ritual obligation (śrāddha and funeral rites) as the foundation of inheritance entitlement

mentions.quote: Because a son saves his father from the hell called Put, one should strive for his birth
The ancestors, fearing a fall into hell, long for sons, thinking: 'Someone who will go to Gayā, he will save us.'
for the sake of the funeral cake and water rites, and for the proclamation of his name in *dharma*

themes.justification: The text grounds inheritance entitlement not merely in blood ties but in ritual capacity — the ability to offer the funeral cake is the spiritual justification for the legal right to inherit.

themes.topic: The legal status and property rights of women (wives and daughters)

mentions.quote: the wife is remembered as half the body, equal in the fruit of merit and demerit
The wife is the taker of the husband's wealth; without her, the daughter is remembered as the heir
Even if of good conduct, and even when a share is made, a woman does not deserve immovable property

themes.justification: A sustained thematic thread across sections 1.26.8–1.26.12, balancing the wife's identity as 'half the body' against her restricted ownership of land and movable property.

mentions.quote: Sons of many kinds were made by the ancient sages
Thirteen sons have been stated by Manu of old
The son of the field is condemned by the good, and likewise the son of a remarried woman

themes.justification: Section 1.26.7 is devoted entirely to enumerating and ranking twelve or thirteen recognized types of sons, from the legitimate son to the rejected, bought, and self-given son.

themes.topic: Royal authority as the residual heir and enforcer of legal order

mentions.quote: the king is the taker of their wealth, for he is the lord of all
he should be established in his own share by the king and punished as a persistent offender
the king should examine daily the disputes brought by litigants

themes.justification: The king appears as both the ultimate escheator when no qualified heirs exist and the judicial authority who enforces partition agreements and punishes fraudulent gamblers.

themes.topic: Regulation and moral ambivalence toward gambling

mentions.quote: Gambling was forbidden by Manu as it destroys truth, purity, and wealth; but it was permitted by others, accompanied by a share for the king
Wicked men who play with false dice, and those who withhold the king's share

themes.justification: Chapter 1.27 opens by registering disagreement between Manu's prohibition and other authorities' regulated permission, then proceeds to frame gambling as a legally supervised activity.

themes.topic: Supremacy of the Veda and Manu as the ultimate standard for Smṛti

mentions.quote: Because it is connected to the meaning of the Veda, the pre-eminence of Manu is remembered. A Smṛti that is contrary to the meaning of Manu is not to be praised

themes.justification: The closing verse of the entire work articulates a meta-jurisprudential principle: Manu's authority derives from its consonance with Vedic meaning, making this the text's final theoretical statement on legal epistemology.

themes.topic: Punishment theory: gradation of penalties according to person, fault, and capacity

mentions.quote: Verbal censure, reprimand, fine, and capital punishment—the fourfold punishment has been devised. Having known the person, the fault, and his means, one should apply it
One should first apply verbal punishment, and after that, reprimand; the third is a monetary fine, and after that, capital punishment

themes.justification: Section 1.29 introduces a formal four-tier theory of punishment applied progressively, with explicit attention to the offender's social standing as a variable — a coherent penal jurisprudence.

themes.topic: Eschatological anxiety as motivator for son-production and ritual compliance

mentions.quote: The ancestors, fearing a fall into hell, long for sons
a father with a bad son sinks into blinding darkness

themes.justification: The recurring invocation of hell (Put), darkness, and ancestral fear functions as an implicit ideological mechanism that makes the entire inheritance and sonship law emotionally urgent beyond its legal formality.

citations.quote: Gambling was forbidden by Manu as it destroys truth, purity, and wealth
citations.justification: Manu's prohibition of gambling is cited as the prior authoritative ruling, against which an alternative permissive tradition is contrasted.

citations.quote: Thirteen sons have been stated by Manu of old
citations.justification: Bṛhaspati defers to Manu's enumeration of thirteen son-types as the foundational classification that his own discussion follows and refines.

citations.quote: the pre-eminence of Manu is remembered. A Smṛti that is contrary to the meaning of Manu is not to be praised
citations.justification: The closing verse explicitly elevates Manu's Smṛti as the supreme normative standard for all other Smṛti texts, grounding his authority in Vedic consonance.

citations.quote: Having worshipped Agni and Prajāpati, she is made so, said Gautama
citations.justification: Gautama is named as the source authority for the ritual procedure of appointing a daughter as a substitute heir, indicating a citation to the Gautamadharmasūtra tradition.

citations.quote: all of it for one without son, father, or wife—thus says Śaunaka
citations.justification: Śaunaka is cited by the explicit attribution formula 'thus says Śaunaka' to authorize the rule that a non-kin cremator takes the entire estate of a person without any heirs.
